issues.legal_issue: A conviction for multiple murders cannot be sustained on related eyewitness testimony that is neither wholly reliable nor wholly unreliable when the testimony requires material corroboration and the other evidence does not reliably corroborate it.
material_facts: The prosecution relied principally on two eyewitnesses who were closely related to the deceased and one accused.

The witnesses could potentially have seen some assaults, but the site-plans and the witnesses’ accounts made it difficult to accept that they saw the assaults on all the deceased; the investigating officer also acknowledged that their alleged hiding places were not recorded in the site-plan.
The arrests and recoveries were doubtful, the alleged motive was not established for two accused and was weak for the other, and available independent witnesses were not examined.
Other circumstances also cast doubt on the prosecution account, including the absence of fingerprint and dog-squad reports and contradictions about who went to the police station.
issues.conclusion: The prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The convictions and death sentences of the three appellants were unsustainable and were set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Related or interested testimony must be scrutinised with care, but relationship alone does not make it unreliable: Piara Singh v. State of Punjab. A witness who is not wholly reliable may require independent corroboration in material particulars: Anil Phukan v. State of Assam. Evidence that is neither wholly reliable nor wholly unreliable requires such corroboration: Vadivelu Thevar v. State of Madras. The prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, and courts must assess evidence by its intrinsic worth and probabilities rather than conjecture: State of Rajasthan v. Teja Singh and State of Punjab v. Jagir Singh. The judgment also emphasised heightened scrutiny when courts consider a death sentence.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_conviction and related_eyewitnesses_not_wholly_reliable and material_corroboration_absent and prosecution_evidence_leaves_reasonable_doubt

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.related_eyewitnesses_not_wholly_reliable: The prosecution relies on eyewitnesses connected to the deceased or accused whose testimony is not wholly reliable.
predicates.material_corroboration_absent: The testimony requiring corroboration is not supported in material particulars by reliable direct or circumstantial evidence.
predicates.prosecution_evidence_leaves_reasonable_d: The evidence as a whole leaves a reasonable doubt about the accused’s guilt.
predicates.conviction_and_death_sentence_set_aside: The conviction and any death sentence based on it are set aside.

issues.definition: When a criminal conviction appeal depends on related eyewitnesses who are not wholly reliable, material corroboration is absent, and the evidence leaves reasonable doubt, the conviction and any death sentence are set aside.

issues.legal_issue: Information supplied by an accused in custody is admissible as discovery evidence only to the extent that it distinctly relates to a fact discovered, and recoveries from places accessible to all cannot reliably corroborate guilt in the circumstances of this case.
material_facts: The prosecution relied on an arrest-cum-recovery memo recording statements that the accused had committed the murders and could produce the weapons.
No public witness named in the memo was examined to support the recoveries.
One weapon was recovered from a room and the others from an open field behind the place of the murders, places accessible to others.
The alleged bloodstained clothes were not recovered on a memorandum of the accused, and the forensic reports concerning them were inconclusive.
issues.conclusion: The statements about committing the crime were not admissible as discovery information, and the circumstances of the recoveries did not permit reliance on them; the clothes could not be used against the accused as discovery evidence.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, only information that distinctly relates to the fact discovered is admissible; a confession or account of past use is not made admissible merely because it accompanies discovery. Pulukuri Kottayya v. King Emperor explains that the discovered fact includes the place of discovery and the accused’s knowledge of it. The Court considered the absence of supporting public witnesses and the accessibility of the recovery locations in assessing whether the recoveries could be relied on.

predicates.criminal_trial_relies_on_discovery_recov: The prosecution in a criminal trial relies on objects allegedly recovered following information from an accused in custody.
predicates.custodial_statement_includes_confession: The information attributed to the accused includes a confession or an account of committing the offence beyond the fact of discovery.
predicates.recovery_place_accessible_to_others: The object is recovered from a place accessible to people other than the accused.
predicates.confessional_statement_inadmissible_and_: The confession is not admissible as discovery information and the recovery cannot be relied on as reliable corroboration.

issues.definition: When a criminal trial relies on discovery recoveries, the custodial statement includes a confession, and the recovery place is accessible to others, the confession is inadmissible as discovery information and the recovery is not reliable corroboration.

issues.legal_issue: The accused’s failure to explain facts within special knowledge does not relieve the prosecution of its obligation to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
material_facts: The State argued that the accused had not discharged their burden and had not explained matters in their statements under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
The Court found that the prosecution had not first proved the case beyond reasonable doubt.
issues.conclusion: The accused’s failure to explain could not make up for the prosecution’s failure to prove its case, and the burden did not shift to the accused.
issues.legal_principle: The prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt before the burden concerning facts within the accused’s special knowledge under Section 106 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 can shift. Section 106 does not relieve the prosecution of its burden: Joydeb Patra v. State of West Bengal, relying on Sucha Singh v. State of Punjab and Vikramjit Singh v. State of Punjab. The prosecution must stand on its own evidence, and a weak defence cannot cure a failure of proof: Anand Ramachandra Chougule v. Sidarai Laxman Chougala, which also refers to Sunil Kundu v. State of Jharkhand.

predicates.criminal_proceeding: The proceeding is a criminal case in which the prosecution bears the burden of proving guilt.
predicates.prosecution_has_not_proved_guilt_beyond_: The prosecution has not established the accused’s guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
predicates.accused_has_not_explained_special_knowle: The accused has not explained facts said to be within their special knowledge.
predicates.burden_does_not_shift_to_accused: The accused’s failure to explain does not shift the burden or cure the prosecution’s failure of proof.

issues.definition: If the prosecution has not proved guilt beyond reasonable doubt in a criminal proceeding, the accused’s failure to explain facts within special knowledge does not shift the burden to the accused.

issues.legal_issue: An appeal challenging an acquittal cannot succeed when the prosecution evidence does not establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
material_facts: The first informant appealed against the High Court’s acquittal of an accused.

The Court found the prosecution case insufficient to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, including because the evidence of the eyewitnesses was not wholly reliable and was not adequately corroborated.
issues.conclusion: The appeal against the acquittal was dismissed as without merit.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the requirement that the prosecution prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt and concluded that the evidence did not establish guilt. The judgment does not state a separate standard for appellate review of an acquittal.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging an acquittal in a criminal case.
predicates.prosecution_evidence_does_not_prove_guil: The prosecution evidence does not establish the accused’s guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an acquittal but the prosecution evidence does not prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, the acquittal is upheld.
